events.text: You hang the banner at the head of the White Stairs, where every envoy must climb past it. Grey silk, one line of ink: all the isles under one hand. Within the hour a cloud-barge from each faction is circling to read it, and an old tea-seller on the lowest landing quietly takes down her price board and shuts her shop.

choices.text: Let them read it, and say nothing

effects.log: You let them circle until dusk. By night three factions have written, and not one letter uses the word polite.

choices.text: Send each faction a hand-inked copy

effects.log: It takes your scribes a week. The envoys are insulted and flattered in equal parts, and they remember your handwriting.

events.text: {auh4_held} regions of sixteen are yours tonight, which is to say none, and your seat has gone very quiet about it. The Lantern-Keeper from the lower terrace asks only whether the isles are to be conquered or collected. You find you have not decided, and that an unwritten answer is the most dangerous thing a banner can fly over.

choices.text: "Collected. Conquest is for people with no patience."

effects.log: The Lantern-Keeper writes that down and goes away smiling. It is repeated in the halls by morning, with embellishments.

choices.text: "Whichever the isle prefers."

effects.log: You see on the old keeper's face that this is the wrong answer and also the one that will be quoted.

events.text: The first barges leave harbour at dawn with the banner on the lead mast: spirit stones in the hold, a hundred sword-disciples on deck, and a cook who has packed far too much. Below you the Sea of Clouds is a bright floor, and {auh4_region} a smudge on its rim, held by {auh4_foe}, who has not yet heard that anyone is coming.

choices.text: Stand at the prow the whole way

effects.log: You stand until your robes are wet through with cloud. The disciples decide you are either very brave or have forgotten how to sit.

choices.text: Go below and study the isle charts again

effects.log: The charts carry a margin note in a hand you do not know: the western reefs sing at night. You pass this on, and it saves a barge.

events.text: A small crowd waits at the wharf of the last friendly isle. Mothers with satchels of dried plum, a smith with a sword he wants carried, an old disciple asking whether the fighting will reach the herb terraces. You answer them one by one, and the barge leaves an hour late and a good deal heavier with gifts.

choices.text: Carry the smith's sword, and say whose it is

effects.log: The blade is plain and well made. You promise it will come home. You are going to have to keep that promise.

choices.text: Leave on time; the tide will not wait

effects.log: The crowd waves anyway. Nobody is cross, but a small knot of faces turns away before the barge clears the pier.

events.text: The way is a long climb of cloud-stairs, isle to isle, and {auh4_power} has had a month to make the stairs worse. Half the bridges are cut; the rest are watched. Your vanguard sits down on a mooring post to wait for orders. A young disciple says quietly that the ropes were cut by someone who wanted them to look cut.

choices.text: Follow the ropes: a friend has been here

effects.log: The knots lead to a watcher on a dry shelf, who has waited a long time to be asked for a side. The road ahead may be easier than it looks.

choices.text: Order the bridges mended and move at night

effects.log: It takes all night and costs nothing but sleep. At dawn the first of the guard are astonished to find you already across.

events.text: A year on the cloud-front, and the ground is the same width as the year before. {auh4_foe} keeps the passes and your barges keep the sky. The disciples cook on deck and sing loudly to avoid thinking about the long gap in the next ridge, where the wind has never been trusted. You could press the ridge. You could dig in. You could, though your officers would call it soft, spare the little isle under it.

choices.text: Press the ridge before the season turns

effects.log: You commit three barges and your best sword-line. The ridge is yours by nightfall, and some of it is paid for the next day.

choices.text: Hold the line and let the winter work

effects.log: It is a very dull winter. Your stores stay full and theirs do not, and no song is made of it.

choices.text: Spare the little isle under the ridge

effects.log: The isle has two hundred farmers and a shrine to a goat. You send word it will not be touched, and a surprising number of other isles hear that too.

events.text: Scouts bring in a prisoner from {auh4_region}: a company-commander of the defenders, bruised, furious, sixteen years old. His unit has had no rice in a week, he says, and if you would only let them walk out they would not fight you again. Your officers want the pass tonight. The boy asks for a drink of water.

choices.text: Give the water, and take the pass at dawn

effects.log: You do both. The boy drinks, and tells you which plank of the north gate is rotten. You are not sure you wanted to be told.

choices.text: Feed the beaten company too, and camp where you are

effects.log: Food crosses the line under a white cloth. By morning half their company has put down its swords for good.

choices.text: Let him go back with a warning

effects.log: He goes. {auh4_foe} receives your message and moves nothing. The year passes without change.

events.text: Spring thunder comes early over the front, and every fire-spirit banked in your barges goes out at once. The defenders have plainly planned for this. Their drums start on the high shelf while your guard fumbles with their lamps, and in the dark your officers argue about whether this is a moment to run forward or to be very, very still.

choices.text: Run forward under the drums

effects.log: You go, with the first line, without light. It is the loudest and strangest hour of the year, and the shelf is yours before the second drum.

choices.text: Be very still, and let the thunder pass

effects.log: You sit under damp silk for three hours. Nothing happens to anyone. Years later it is still your best-remembered decision.

choices.text: Send word to the shelf that the thunder is yours too

effects.log: It is a bluff, and it works for a day. A town on the lower isle opens its gates while the thunder is still ringing.

events.text: The last flag of {auh4_region} comes down on a still evening. {auh4_foe} stands in the Hall of the Shelf and gives up the keys one at a time, and takes a long while about it. Your disciples cheer. Then they notice the defenders are not afraid of them at all, and the cheering thins.

choices.text: Take the keys, and say thank you

effects.log: It is an odd thing to say and it is repeated. The defenders talk of it for a season.

choices.text: Hand the keys back, to keep for you

effects.log: It is a risk. The old commander looks at them a long time. Then {auh4_foe} salutes, a little late.

events.text: {auh4_region} is yours, and {auh4_held} regions of sixteen now fly the grey silk. On the dock the tea-seller from the White Stairs, who has followed the barges on her own account, sets up her kettle again and says nobody has paid her to leave yet.

choices.text: Pay for the tea, and ask the news

effects.log: She charges double and gives you back nine facts, seven of them useful.

choices.text: Name her Keeper of the Isle's Kettles

effects.log: It is a joke, written out as a decree. She treats it as one and puts it on her sign.

events.text: Half the defenders of {auh4_region} do not wait to be told: they cross over the day the isle falls, bringing their drill-books and their tea. Your veterans eye them sourly. A boy of fifteen says aloud that they were only guarding their own roofs, and a veteran of {auh4_power} looks away and does not contradict him.

choices.text: Put them in your front rank

effects.log: It is a hard thing to do to a person and they know it. They fight harder than anyone, and their names are on your muster rolls by year's end.

choices.text: Send them home with their drill-books

effects.log: They go home and spread the story of what you did. The next isle opens its gates before you can finish the words.

events.text: The year ends badly. Two barges gone, a third stranded on a shoal, and {auh4_foe} sends a polite letter with an exact count of your dead. You are alive. The banner is wrapped and leaning in a corner. A banner, you think, is a thing that always costs most to the one who raised it.

choices.text: Write back, and answer every figure with a name

effects.log: It does not change the arithmetic. It changes you.

choices.text: Hang the banner back up, a little lower

effects.log: It is a quiet gesture. The disciples notice, and some take more heart from the lower banner than they ever did from the high.

events.text: Your sword-line was strong, but the isle had its own weather, and the weather was theirs. The survivors drift home in twos and threes, ashamed, wet and hungry. An old disciple, one you did not want to bring, is last in with a wounded boy on his back, saying only that he is sorry the line broke.

choices.text: Say the line was never his to hold

effects.log: He weeps, which you did not expect, and nobody else in the hall can look at him. The boy lives.

choices.text: Order a feast anyway

effects.log: There is nothing to eat. There is a feast. People remember that you tried.

events.text: {auh4_power} counters you so completely that your whole plan reads like a lesson in what not to do. You spend a week alone with the isle charts. On the seventh night, in the margin of the very last, you find a note: a date, a name, and the single word "later". You do not know who wrote it.

choices.text: Keep the chart, and wait

effects.log: You wait. It is not a peaceful wait. It teaches you something useful about yourself.

choices.text: Burn the chart, and begin again

effects.log: You begin again from a clean sheet. It is fast, hard, and for a while quite pleasant.

events.text: The Jade Seat of {auh4_power} stands at the top of the last stair, above the cloud-floor, and before it waits {auh4_foe}. No army, no herald: a cushion on bare stone and a pot of tea gone cold. The defenders on the walls look down and do not move. It is a courtesy, you understand. For the last time, a person is allowed to refuse a war.

choices.text: Climb the stair and take the cushion by force

ok.log: The stair is long and the exchange short. When it ends, the defenders on the wall lower their flags in order of rank.

fail.log: Halfway up the stair you see how long this has been prepared. You are driven back down it with your guard watching in silence.

choices.text: Sit, and speak of terms over the cold tea

effects.log: You drink the tea. It is dreadful. A treaty in nineteen lines is written on the back of an old tea-house menu.

events.text: {auh4_foe} does not come to the gate. Instead the shelf is laid out like a dinner table: bridges rolled back, towers hung with lamps, and one path of white stones climbing to the Seat. It is the most beautiful trap you have ever seen. You can see exactly where the hidden wires are, and that is part of the invitation.

choices.text: Walk the white path and spring every wire

ok.log: You walk, and the wires sing, and the lamps go out one by one. At the top the Seat is waiting, and so is the bow.

fail.log: You walk the white path. At the fourth lamp you realise you are a good deal less alone than you thought.

choices.text: Send word you will take terms, and a good meal

effects.log: The feast is better than the battle would have been. The treaty is signed between two courses.

events.text: The outer isles fell in the field, and the capital stands bare. The Seat of {auh4_power} has no one to shut its gates; the defenders have quietly gone home. You come to the top of the last stair carrying the banner yourself. The guard of honour is three old men and a cat.

choices.text: Hang the banner there, and bow to the cat

effects.log: The cat is not impressed. The three old men are, a little. They give you the keys unasked.

choices.text: Read the names of the fallen from the stair

effects.log: It takes an hour. The old men listen to all of it, and one of them takes off his hat.

events.text: No battle at the Seat. You find its great doors open and its tea laid, and on the cushion a short letter in a firm hand: {auh4_foe} has left in the night, and takes the blame for everything done in defence. You read it twice. A banner is a heavy thing to carry into an emptied room.

choices.text: Keep the letter, and look for the author

effects.log: The author is found two isles away, mending a fence. You do not speak. You hang a lamp on the post.

choices.text: Seat the nearest honest clerk

effects.log: The clerk is horrified. The Seat runs better than it has in years.

events.text: Word comes from {auh4_region}, one of the isles you hold: the grey silk is down from the harbour mast, a green one hung in its place, and your garrison is sitting on the quay with its boots in the water. The headman has put out a plain statement. They would like to be asked, next time.

choices.text: Send the host, and take the mast down

effects.log: The host goes. The green silk is cut, and nothing else. It is quiet for a year after, and the quiet has a bruise in it.

choices.text: Go yourself, and listen

effects.log: You sit in the headman's kitchen for two days. The isle keeps its flag; you keep the harbour. Nobody calls it victory.

choices.text: Ask the garrison what they did first

effects.log: They were stealing the isle's herbs. You say so, publicly, and replace the whole garrison.

events.text: The headmen of {auh4_region} have organised a boycott of your spirit-stone assessors, and the assessors, mostly honest clerks, are being fed very polite meals by people who then refuse to speak to them. By the third week the clerks are fat and miserable and the stones unpaid. It is the most civilised revolt you have ever seen.

choices.text: Replace the assessors with sword-disciples

effects.log: The stones arrive within the week. So does a notice, delivered by a child, that the isle will remember.

choices.text: Cut the assessment by a third, and announce it

effects.log: You lose the stones and gain a rumour. It is the better of the two.

choices.text: Send a single clerk, with no escort

effects.log: She comes home with half the stones and a sack of pickled plums. It is a start.

events.text: Young sword-disciples from {auh4_region} have seized the old watchtower there, under banners with nothing written on them. They want to leave the long war without being called deserters. Their leader, a girl of nineteen, has put the key to the tower in a teapot and sits on the stair with the pot in her lap.

choices.text: Break the tower, and take the teapot

effects.log: The tower is broken in an afternoon. The key is pocketed. Nobody there is quite the same again.

choices.text: Let them leave, with their swords

effects.log: They go with their swords and a note. Over the next year, two of them send a handsome gift.

choices.text: Ask first what the war cost them

effects.log: The answer fills six hours. You can do nothing about any of it, and you remember all of it.

events.text: A white barge, no banner, sets down on the topmost shelf of your seat in the full light of noon. The one who steps off has no shadow. It speaks without moving its mouth: all the factions are one, and the gods have noticed. Mujin, Noegong and Unmyeong send an offer. Kneel, and the isles may keep their small laws. Refuse, and be measured.

choices.text: Kneel, and let the isles have their peace

effects.log: You kneel on the cold shelf. The shadowless herald nods once. The isles are quiet for ten thousand years and never learn your name.

choices.text: "Tell them I have not finished."

effects.log: The herald looks at you a long moment. Then the white barge lifts, silent, and the clouds do not move for a day.

events.text: A hush lies over the isles. Every cloud has stopped moving. A cold light settles at the foot of the White Stairs and shapes itself into a figure of no particular face, which says it has come on behalf of the gods. Sixteen regions under one hand is not a thing the heavens allow. It will not be argued with. It will only wait.

choices.text: Bow, and ask what peace costs

effects.log: The figure names the price in a voice like a door closing. You pay it. The isles are saved, and your name will not be spoken.

choices.text: Stand, and hold the banner higher

effects.log: The figure bows, which is worse than any threat. It rises into the cloud. Your hands shake for the rest of the evening.

events.text: On the night before, you walk the whole length of your seat, from the tea-terraces to the sword-court, and every window is lit. Your people know what is coming. An old cook leaves a bowl at your elbow without a word. The wind is wrong and the stars are in the wrong order, and for the first time in your long life you are glad of all of it.

choices.text: Spend the night with the people who stayed

effects.log: You listen until dawn. They tell you little that is wise and everything that is true. At first light you go out to the sky, lighter.

choices.text: Spend the night at the sword-court, alone

effects.log: You work through every form you know, slowly, then fast, then slowly again. By dawn your hands are quiet.

events.text: A letter arrives at midnight from the tea-seller of the White Stairs. It has one line and a pressed flower: "Whatever you do, eat first." You read it three times. You eat. The porridge is cold and excellent. Afterwards you stand at the edge of the highest shelf and look at the whole broken dazzle of the cloud-sea, and decide it was worth the trouble.

choices.text: Write back, and keep the flower

effects.log: You write four lines. They go down on the first barge. The flower lives in your sleeve for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Burn the letter, and finish the porridge

effects.log: It is a practical choice. The ash is warm, and so are you.

events.text: {auh4_god} comes down on the Sea of Clouds with the sound of a thousand banners snapping at once. It does not speak. It lifts one hand, and the sea beneath it becomes a table of beaten gold. You see now what is meant by a god: not strength, but the whole sky agreeing with one person.

choices.text: Meet it on the gold, and strike first

ok.log: Your blade rings. The gold cracks like ice. The god steps back one pace, the first it has ever taken backward, and the sky shudders.

fail.log: The gold holds. You are thrown the length of the sky and land on a roof three isles away, with no sword and a ringing in your teeth.

choices.text: Let it come, and break the table under it

ok.log: You wait. The god lifts its hand, and you open a hole in the world beneath its feet. It is the best thing you ever thought of.

fail.log: You wait too long. The gold becomes a wall, and the wall a ceiling, and nobody has ever described what came next.

events.text: The second descent is quieter. {auh4_god} stands on the rim of your seat with the whole white sky behind, and all your disciples kneel without being told. You alone are on your feet. The god asks, mildly, why. You say you do not know. It is the truest thing you have said in a century.

choices.text: "Because I am tired of kneeling."

ok.log: The god laughs, a sound like many bells. The fight is long and entirely in the sky, and you come down in ribbons with the god bowing from a cloud.

fail.log: The god does not laugh. The fight is short, and ends with you on the floor of your own sword-court while your disciples carefully look elsewhere.

choices.text: Say nothing, and draw

ok.log: The draw is the only answer you have, and it is a good one. The cloud splits along its length, and for the first time the sky has a seam.

fail.log: You draw, and the god is already inside the draw, patient as weather. Everything after that is a long fall.

events.text: The last god comes at night, wrapped in no light at all. The isles dim wherever it passes. It tells you without sound that every one before it was only a test of your reach, and that it has come to measure what is left. Your disciples are asleep. You step out onto the stair alone.

choices.text: Meet it in the dark, and strike by ear

ok.log: There is no sight to rely on, only the old forms in the old order, and your breath. Something in the dark gives way, and a dawn begins.

fail.log: You listen for it so hard that you hear only yourself. The dark takes the rest.

choices.text: Light every lamp of the seat at once

ok.log: The light is brief and bright and enormous. The god flinches, and in that flinch is the whole chance of the world. You take it.

fail.log: The lamps flare. Then they go out together, and the dark has your name.

events.text: Mujin does not come, nor Noegong, nor Unmyeong. The sky above the White Stairs is a plain sky now, and the clouds cross it at their own pace. Sixteen regions under one hand, and nothing above that. You stand at the edge of the highest shelf and, for the first time, have no one to answer to. The tea-seller brings you a cup and says it is on the house.

choices.text: Take the cup, and drink

effects.log: It is the best tea of your life. You sit until dusk and watch the sky be nothing in particular.

choices.text: Pour it out over the edge, for the others

effects.log: The tea drifts into the cloud-sea. You do not know who it is for. Probably all of them.

events.text: Years later they will say it happened in a single morning. In truth it took eleven years and many deaths, and you remember each. But the morning is the part that sticks: grey silk on every mast, no shadow on the stairs, and the long clear wind that comes when nobody above you is listening. You are free to leave the seat, finally. You do not.

choices.text: Stay, and keep the isles as they are

effects.log: You keep them as they are, which turns out to be harder than conquering them. For a long time it is a pleasant sort of struggle.

choices.text: Walk out onto the open sky, and keep walking

effects.log: The isles let you go. Behind you a tea-seller reopens her shop. Ahead of you is everything else.

events.text: The god's blow does not feel like a blow. It feels like the whole sky deciding something about you, and then quiet. You see the White Stairs once more from above, small and bright, with the banner still on its mast. Someone will take that banner down tomorrow. Someone else, much later, will put it back up.

choices.text: Let go, and look at the isles

effects.log: You look at them all the way down. They are very beautiful from far enough away.

choices.text: Reach for the banner, once more

effects.log: Your hand closes on nothing. It was worth trying.

events.text: You are not killed. You are put back in your proper place, which is a good deal below where you stood. The sky closes. The banner is taken down by a god's patient hand. Sixteen regions go back to their own, and nobody kneels and nobody cheers. The isles are all still there. Only you are different.

choices.text: Accept it, and go quietly

effects.log: You go. The isles are quiet for the rest of your life. Nobody speaks of it, and everybody remembers.

choices.text: Remember it, and tell the next disciples

effects.log: You do. It becomes a tale. It is told wrong, and it is told for ten thousand years.

events.text: The white barge lifts off the topmost shelf and takes the weather with it. Your people line the rail and watch it go. A fine rain begins, the first in months. Sixteen regions, one hand, and a very long peace that nobody will remember being earned. An old disciple says it is what a good peace is: unremarked.

choices.text: Sit in the rain, and let it fall

effects.log: You sit. It is a good rain. You are not unhappy, and you are not altogether sure what you are.

choices.text: Order the lamps lit in honour of the quiet

effects.log: They are lit. For ten thousand years the isles will light them on this night, not knowing why.

events.text: You bowed, and the sky lifted, and nothing else changed. The tea-sellers sold tea, the sword-disciples drilled, the herb-gardens were weeded. Somewhere above, a very large decision was made and written in a book you will never see. You look at your hands. They are the same hands. A year ago you could not have said this would be enough.

choices.text: Let it be enough

effects.log: It is enough. It is a long, quiet, ordinary happiness, and you are surprised how little it asks of you.

choices.text: Write the whole history down, as it was

effects.log: You write it. It is the only record of what you nearly did, and nobody reads it for centuries.

events.text: The grey silk comes down off the mast in a single movement, and a young disciple folds it corner to corner, the way a burial flag is folded. The sixteen regions are released. A few cheer. A few weep. The tea-seller looks up from her cart, nods once, and goes back to sorting leaves.

choices.text: Keep the folded silk

effects.log: It lives in a chest at the foot of your bed, and you look at it on certain nights.

choices.text: Give it to the disciple who folded it

effects.log: The disciple is speechless. It hangs over their door for years, as a sign of something.

events.text: You take the banner down yourself, without ceremony, in the evening. The isles do not notice at first. Then someone on the lower terrace sees the empty mast and puts a hand to their mouth. By midnight the whole realm knows. Your officers wait to be told if it is a defeat. You say it is a change of weather.

choices.text: Take a long walk along the edge of the sky

effects.log: You walk for three days. You come back lighter.

choices.text: Stay at your desk and answer every letter

effects.log: The letters are mostly kind. A few are not. You answer all of them.

events.text: You raise the standard in the Hall of Prayers of your own domain, and the offerings on the altar tremble in their bowls. A bare white cloth: every pantheon, one order. The lesser gods who hear it feel it in their names. A small god of crossroads, three thousand years at his post, quietly takes to his heels.

choices.text: Let the offerings settle, and say nothing

effects.log: They settle. The silence in the hall is felt in the temples below, and for a night the worshippers pray in whispers.

choices.text: Proclaim it to every temple at once

effects.log: It travels by prayer, and by morning every pantheon has its answer ready, half of it drafted in verse.

events.text: {auh4_held} of sixteen domains are yours, which is to say none, and the Book of Fates has already begun to redraw a margin. The Keeper of Names comes to you with one respectful question: if all the pantheons are one, who then receives the prayers? You have no answer, and an unanswered prayer is the most dangerous thing in any world.

choices.text: "Each as before. I take nothing from the altars."

effects.log: The Keeper writes it down. Whether it is true, no one can yet say, but it is quoted in every temple by morning.

choices.text: "Every prayer to every god will pass through me."

effects.log: The Keeper does not write that down. Nobody needs to. It is said, and it spreads.

events.text: The procession leaves your domain at the hour when the sun is a coin on the horizon. Lesser gods march in the van with their symbols raised: a lamp, a loom, a plough. The believers of your temples walk behind, three thousand voices. Ahead lies {auh4_region}, held by {auh4_foe}, who is still receiving offerings and has not been warned.

choices.text: Walk at the head, in plain robes

effects.log: The lesser gods are scandalised. The believers are not. The first night, a girl offers you her entire supper, and you eat it.

choices.text: Read the Book of Fates again on the road

effects.log: There is a blank line in it where {auh4_foe} should be. You do not know what that means, and it is useful to be afraid of it.

events.text: A shrine-keeper from the last friendly domain runs out onto the road with an armful of paper charms. Every worshipper in her village has written one, and she asks that you carry them. They are blessings, and requests, and a few small curses on your enemies in the careful hand of children. You carry them in a sack and read them on the way.

choices.text: Read one aloud each night to the host

effects.log: They begin to look forward to it. By the fourth night the host knows the villagers by name.

choices.text: Seal the sack, unread

effects.log: You keep your word and your counsel. The sack stays at the foot of your bed and does not stop being heavy.

events.text: {auh4_power} has had a month to prepare the road. Every wayside shrine on the way to {auh4_region} has been quietly repurposed: offerings swept off, the altar turned to face the wrong way. The host halts at the first, uncertain. A young priest says a god cannot be insulted by a turned altar, only by those who turn it.

choices.text: Turn the altars back, one by one, as you pass

effects.log: It takes a day for each. At the sixth shrine the believers join in with brooms. You gain a following you did not ask for.

choices.text: March past, and leave them turned

effects.log: The host does as ordered. Behind you the shrines stay as they are, and a hundred small believers look after you with bewildered faces.

events.text: A year on the borders of {auh4_region}, and the line has not moved. {auh4_foe} commands the domain from a height of fog, and your lesser gods fight with prayers, blessings and floods of omen. Nothing decisive, nothing safe. The Keeper of Names suggests a bold push at the sacred spring. He also suggests, with less hope, that you might wait for the spring to move.

choices.text: Push to the sacred spring

effects.log: You push, and the spring, long sacred, is fouled by the fighting. Both sides are ashamed. You hold it nonetheless.

choices.text: Hold, and let the faith of the domain wear thin

effects.log: It takes the year. When it is over, the temples there have emptied by a third.

choices.text: Spare the small shrines of the border

effects.log: You send word that no altar will be touched. Three villages bring offerings the next morning, carefully set on the road.

events.text: A lesser god of the domain, beaten in the night, is brought before you, a god of wells, not much taller than a child. Their followers watch from a distance. The god says very quietly that they have not wanted this war in three thousand years, and ask only that their wells stay clean. Your captains want the pass by dawn.

choices.text: Keep the wells, and take the pass

effects.log: The wells are kept clean. The pass is taken, and the little god of wells hums as it is led away.

choices.text: Release them, and trust their word

effects.log: They go, and the wells of the pass go quiet. Whether this is peace, no one is sure.

choices.text: Hold the line, and let the god sit beside you

effects.log: They sit, and by evening are telling your captains where every stream runs. It is a better map than any.

events.text: In the third season the Book of Fates records a reversal you did not cause. An incense-fire in an obscure temple caught the wrong wind, and three of your best lesser gods lost their names for a day. Nobody blames anyone. The believers pray harder. A lamp-keeper asks, very reasonably, what the plan is for the next harvest.

choices.text: Press on while the enemy is also confused

effects.log: You press, in a fog of unfamiliar names, and win more by luck than design. Nobody is prouder.

choices.text: Call back the host, and rewrite the plan

effects.log: You spend a month rewriting. When it is done it is shorter, plainer, and much better.

choices.text: Send the lamp-keeper the plan, and ask for edits

effects.log: He sends back four pages in a neat hand. Two are useful. One is a poem.

events.text: The last altar of {auh4_region} is cleared, and the lamp lit on it burns in your name. {auh4_foe} comes out of the sanctuary and sets a crown of dried barley on your head, which is the old custom. It is not a surrender. It is, you suspect, a sort of apology, and the lesser gods weep with embarrassment.

choices.text: Wear the crown for the evening

effects.log: It scratches. You wear it until the last lamp goes out, and the believers love you for it.

choices.text: Hang it on the altar of the domain's own god

effects.log: It is the right thing to do, and you do it unasked. The temple fills with people the next morning.

events.text: {auh4_region} comes into your hand: {auh4_held} of sixteen now. Offerings from its worshippers begin to arrive at your altar the next morning, honey and wheat and a very small bronze bell. The Keeper of Names has to open a new page. He asks, delicately, whether you will accept them. The bell rings once as he says it.

choices.text: Accept every offering, and read each name

effects.log: It takes all night. At dawn you hold the faith of a domain in your palm, and the sense that it is breakable.

choices.text: Send the offerings back with a blessing

effects.log: The domain does not know what to make of that. Its believers write a hymn about it, which is not a good hymn.

events.text: The lesser gods of the conquered domain come over to you in a body, symbols tucked under their arms: a god of beehives, a god of ferries, a god of bad weather. They say, with the shamefaced dignity of the very old, that they only want to keep their altars. Your captains regard them with distrust. The god of ferries asks if the war is nearly done.

choices.text: Welcome them, altars and all

effects.log: The host is dismayed and then charmed. The god of bad weather is put in charge of the baggage train, where he does very well.

choices.text: Set them to guard the road behind you

effects.log: They guard it, grumbling. It is a very safe road for a year.

events.text: The domain holds. Your host is turned back at the sacred spring, and many of your lesser gods are lost to the quiet that follows a failed prayer: names forgotten, altars cold. You walk through the camp that night and read aloud the names you can still remember. There are too many. You stop at the hundredth.

choices.text: Read the rest tomorrow, and the day after

effects.log: You do, for a month. It is slow, and no one asks you to.

choices.text: Light a lamp for each of them

effects.log: The lamps number a thousand. The camp looks like a night market, and the lost would have liked it.

events.text: The defenders of {auh4_region} have a counter you did not think of. They stopped praying. Without prayer, the blessings of your host had nothing to lean on, and the lesser gods who marched under your standard found themselves without a voice. It is a perfectly lawful move. You admire it even as you flee it.

choices.text: Study the counter, and remember it

effects.log: You write it in the margin of the Book of Fates. It is a very small entry, and later quite important.

choices.text: Teach your own lesser gods to be silent

effects.log: It is an odd drill. In the end it holds, and the lesser gods grow fond of the quiet.

events.text: The campaign is lost, and you live. {auh4_foe} sends a long letter, scrupulously fair, ending in one line: "The Book has you down for greater things than this." You cannot tell if it is a taunt. You put it under the lid of the Offering Store and do not mention it.

choices.text: Answer the letter, plainly

effects.log: You answer it, and the answer is also scrupulously fair. It is an odd friendship.

choices.text: Let it lie, and begin again

effects.log: You begin again. The letter stays where you left it and is never lost.

events.text: The Throne Hall of {auh4_power} is a silence in the shape of a hall. {auh4_foe} sits at its centre with no guard and no herald, and the lamps are lit as for an ordinary evening. The offerings are laid, the high priests dismissed. A moment is being offered quite sincerely: refuse the war, or fight it, on the steps of the Throne.

choices.text: Cross the hall and take the Throne

ok.log: The hall rings with the exchange. When it is over the lamps burn steadily in a new order, and the priests return, uncertain.

fail.log: You cross the hall, and the hall does not let you. The Throne is not taken. The lamps go out in order as you leave.

choices.text: Sit, and offer terms across the empty hall

effects.log: You sit in the chair set for you. The terms are written in a single hour, in the plainest hand either of you owns.

events.text: {auh4_foe} sends no army. The whole Throne Hall of {auh4_power} has been emptied and swept, and a single seat set on the bare floor. Above it the Book of Fates lies open at a page that already bears your name. It is the most unnerving thing you have ever been offered: a page you may not turn.

choices.text: Cut the page free of the Book, and take the seat

ok.log: The page comes away in your hand. {auh4_foe} bows, plainly and honestly, and a long age ends.

fail.log: You reach for the page, and the Book closes on your hand. You are put out of the hall with great politeness, and the door is locked behind you.

choices.text: Ask to read the page first, and bargain from there

effects.log: It is a most unusual request. {auh4_foe} grants it. The page, once read, is amended by mutual consent.

events.text: The domains around the Throne have fallen one by one in the field, and the Throne Hall of {auh4_power} stands almost empty. You enter at dusk with only your Keeper of Names. The seat is bare. Its god left at noon, and the lamps are still warm. You put a hand on the cold stone arm of the chair and find it damp.

choices.text: Sit, and wait for dawn

effects.log: You sit until the lamps go out one by one. In the morning the temples below have already begun to pray in your name.

choices.text: Light the lamps again, and leave the seat empty

effects.log: It is a gesture the believers understand without help. The empty seat is honoured for a generation.

events.text: The Throne Hall opens to you without a blow. The defenders have already moved the altars to the cellars, saving what they can. {auh4_foe} left a note in the offering-bowl: the god of the Throne goes into hiding, bearing the blame, and asks only that the worshippers be spared. You read it in a quiet hall with all the incense still burning.

choices.text: Spare the worshippers, and keep the note

effects.log: You post a decree at every gate. The note goes into your robe, over your heart, and stays.

choices.text: Search the cellars for the hidden god

effects.log: You do not find them. You find eleven small altars, each with a candle burning, and set your own beside them.

events.text: A domain you hold, {auh4_region}, has risen. Its temple bells ring at the wrong hour, and its lesser gods have stopped answering the Keeper's roll. The garrison writes that the worshippers have laid a wreath on the old god's empty altar and will not say why. They are, the report says, entirely polite and entirely unmoved.

choices.text: Send the host, and break the wreath

effects.log: The host goes. The wreath is broken, the bells silenced, and a long silence settles on that domain, thick as incense.

choices.text: Go to the altar, and lay a wreath of your own

effects.log: It is the right gesture, though it costs you. The bells ring again, at the proper hour.

choices.text: Ask the Keeper of Names what it is they miss

effects.log: It is a name: a small one, a god of a well. You restore it by decree, and the revolt ends in an afternoon.

events.text: The worshippers of {auh4_region} have stopped making offerings to you. They make them, instead, to nothing: bowls of rice left on empty altars at dawn, quietly gone by evening. A lesser god of your host complains of hunger. The Keeper says it is a lawful boycott, and the Book of Fates has no clause against it.

choices.text: Send the host to fill the bowls itself

effects.log: The host fills them. The domain, humbled and hungry, resumes its offerings, but the gesture lingers.

choices.text: Declare the empty altars a feast day

effects.log: The believers are baffled and then grateful. By evening the bowls are full again, in your name.

choices.text: Fast with them, for a day

effects.log: It is a very long day. When it ends the elders of the domain take you to supper.

events.text: A young priestess of {auh4_region} has gathered half the lesser gods of the domain in the temple court and refuses to open it. She has a staff, a lamp, and a manifesto copied in a hundred hands. You have read it. Nothing in it is false. She would like to be heard before the host is, and asks that her name be written properly.

choices.text: Send the host to clear the court

effects.log: The host clears it. The priestess is taken away, and the manifesto is read in secret for centuries.

choices.text: Go in alone, and let her read it aloud

effects.log: She reads it all. At the end you say it is mostly right, and she is so surprised she sits down.

choices.text: Have the Keeper write her name in the Book

effects.log: The Keeper does so, slowly, with great care. She is a minor god by evening, and a very loyal one.

events.text: The Book of Fates opens by itself on your altar and a page turns. A voice that is not a voice speaks in the margin: every pantheon is one, and the Dao is displeased. There is a Law of Ending, and a Law of Weight, and a Silence older than speech. You are told to kneel to them, or be measured by them. The page waits, with great patience, for your hand.

choices.text: Kneel to the Laws, and let the pantheons rest

effects.log: You kneel. The page closes. For ten thousand years the pantheons keep their small order, and no one remembers who held it together.

choices.text: "Tell the Dao I am not finished."

effects.log: The page turns once more and goes blank. The air in the hall changes, as if the world had paused to listen.

events.text: A silence falls across the sixteen domains. Not a quiet: a silence, as if all sound had been recalled by its owner. At the centre of it, in your own Hall of Prayers, stands a herald made of nothing you can name. It bears no message in words. It simply stands, and you understand the offer in every bone: kneel, and the Laws let you be. Refuse, and be read.

choices.text: Kneel, and accept the Laws' peace

effects.log: You kneel. The silence lifts. The gods go on, a little smaller, and no one knows why.

choices.text: Stand, and speak your own name aloud

effects.log: It is the first thing said in that silence. It does not echo, and it does not need to.

events.text: On the night before, you walk the length of the Hall of Prayers and read, one by one, the names of the lesser gods who followed you. Some are very old. Some are three weeks. A god of small kindnesses leaves a cup of water at your side and a single hand-sewn charm. You tuck it into your sleeve. It weighs nothing.

choices.text: Spend the night among the lesser gods

effects.log: You sit with them until dawn, and nobody says anything grand. At first light you go to meet the Laws, lighter than you have been in ages.

choices.text: Spend the night at the altar, alone

effects.log: You offer nothing, ask nothing, and merely sit. By dawn you have made a kind of peace with the matter.

events.text: A prayer reaches you at midnight, from no one you know, carried on a single breath of incense. "We are afraid, and we are proud." That is all. You read it by the altar lamp. The ink is a child's, the plea unadorned. You decide it is the finest prayer you have ever received.

choices.text: Answer it, in your own hand

effects.log: You write six lines. The incense carries them away, and you never learn who read them.

choices.text: Keep it, and say it back aloud

effects.log: You say it into the empty hall, once, steadily. The hall seems to keep it.

events.text: The Law of Ending arrives without a body: it is the moment every story reaches its last page. The Hall of Prayers goes pale, and every flame in it leans toward you. It does not hurt. It asks, softly, the oldest question: when you have done everything, what are you? You find, to your own surprise, that you have an answer.

choices.text: Answer with the first form you ever learned

ok.log: The form, simple and old, meets {auh4_god} and does not end. It is not a victory so much as a refusal, and it holds.

fail.log: The form is perfect, and perfectly finished. {auh4_god} takes it, and you with it, as the last page takes everything.

choices.text: Answer by lighting a new lamp

ok.log: The lamp lights. {auh4_god} pauses, the way a reader pauses at a chapter break, and you step through.

fail.log: The lamp will not light. You hold the wick until it cools, and then {auh4_god} is upon you.

events.text: The Law of Weight comes in the second hour: every deed you ever did set on a scale, and the scale will not stop. The Hall of Prayers settles into the stone beneath it. You feel, for the first time in an age, your actual weight: the debts, the mercies, the small unkindnesses. It asks which you wish to be measured by.

choices.text: Put it all on the scale, and stand there

ok.log: You stand. The scale sways, and rights, and keeps its balance. The Law is silent, then bows, as one bows to an honest accountant.

fail.log: You stand, and the scale sinks. It is not that you are wicked. It is that you are too heavy, and it takes you down.

choices.text: Add the weight of every name that followed you

ok.log: It is a great deal. The scale shudders and holds, with all of them in it.

fail.log: It is too much. The scale breaks, and you with it, in a shower of names.

events.text: The Silence Before the First Word is the last, and it is not an enemy. It is the thing every prayer is made against. The Hall of Prayers is perfectly still. There is no wind, no flame, no breath. It asks nothing. It only waits to see whether you will speak, and what, and whether anyone will hear.

choices.text: Speak your own name, and let it echo

ok.log: The name rings, and rings, and does not stop. The Silence has met a sound at last, and bends to it.

fail.log: You speak, and the Silence takes the word. You are left with the shape of your mouth and no sound in it.

choices.text: Sing the first hymn you ever heard

ok.log: It is a simple hymn, and it carries. For one breath the Silence is a congregation, and then it is gone.

fail.log: You sing, and no sound emerges. The Silence is perfect. It remains so.

events.text: There is nothing above the Hall of Prayers now but ordinary sky. The Laws still stand as laws, but they stand to one side, as the Dao does for a person who has finished their reading. Every pantheon has sent a delegation. The Keeper of Names, in tears, has brought you the Book of Fates, unlocked. You are, the Keeper says, whatever you decide to be.

choices.text: Take the Book, and write one line in it

effects.log: It is a single line. Nobody reads it for an age. When they do, the world quietly begins again.

choices.text: Give the Book back, unopened

effects.log: The Keeper stares. Then the Keeper smiles, which is rare. The Book is put away for good.

events.text: Every temple bell in the sixteen domains rings at once, then falls silent, then rings again. The believers do not know why. The lesser gods do, and they kneel in the dust of their altars, not to you but to the plain fact of the matter. You walk out through your Gate Shrine into the early light, and for the first time nothing in the world is watching.

choices.text: Walk on, and let the gods go home

effects.log: The gods go home. The believers go home. You walk on, alone, and the road is wider than you imagined.

choices.text: Return to the altar, and light the lamp again

effects.log: It is, at last, only a lamp. It burns as lamps do, and it is enough.

events.text: The Law does not strike. It simply ceases to hold you up. The Hall of Prayers recedes. Your name, the Book says, was never written there, only pencilled, and now rubbed out. The lesser gods look up from their altars as you pass, and you try to remember each of their faces. It is the last work of your attention.

choices.text: Hold each face as long as you can

effects.log: You hold them all the way down. The last you remember is a small god of kindnesses, mouthing a prayer.

choices.text: Look away, toward the empty sky

effects.log: It is vast, clean and unsentimental. You go into it without complaint.

events.text: You fail the Law, and the Law, being just, is not unkind. The domains you held are returned to their old gods with altars intact and offerings restored. The Book of Fates closes on your name. In the Hall of Prayers a lamp burns for you, for a while, and then does not. No one makes a song of it. Everyone knows.

choices.text: Go quietly, and unmourned

effects.log: You go. The believers, who loved you in small ways, pour out a cup in the evening for a very long time.

choices.text: Leave a word with the Keeper of Names

effects.log: The Keeper writes it down. It is a short word. It is, in the end, the one that is remembered.

events.text: The herald dissolves into the incense, and the Hall of Prayers breathes out. Sixteen domains, one order, and a very long peace that nobody will remember being bought. The Keeper of Names says it is the kindest end the Book could have written. You find you agree more than you wanted to.

choices.text: Sit with the Keeper, and share the incense

effects.log: You sit. It is the quietest evening of your life, and you spend it among old friends.

choices.text: Order every altar lit for the length of a night

effects.log: They are lit. For ten thousand years the believers will light them on this night, not knowing why.

events.text: You knelt, the Laws lifted, and nothing else changed. The offerings were laid, the prayers answered, the lamps trimmed, the Book kept. Somewhere in its great margin a decision was entered in a hand you will never read. You look at your own hands in the temple lamp. You thought it would feel like losing.

choices.text: Let the quiet be enough

effects.log: It is enough. It is the gentlest, most ordinary happiness, and you are astonished at how little it asks.

choices.text: Write down the whole story, as it was

effects.log: You write it. It is the only account of how near the pantheons came to being one. Nobody reads it.

events.text: The standard comes down from the Hall of Prayers, and a young priest folds it corner to corner, the way a sacred cloth is folded. The sixteen domains are released. A few lesser gods cheer. A few stand in the doorway and cannot decide. A girl carries the folded cloth to the Offering Store and sets it with the others.

choices.text: Visit the Offering Store, and see it lie there

effects.log: It lies there with the rest. There is some comfort in being one cloth among many.

choices.text: Let the priest keep the standard

effects.log: The priest is astonished. It hangs over the shrine for years, as a sign of something.

events.text: You take the standard down yourself at dusk, with no ceremony. The domains do not notice at first. Then a lamp-keeper sees the bare pole and puts a hand to her mouth. By morning every temple knows. The Keeper of Names waits to be told whether it is a defeat. You tell him it is a change of liturgy.

choices.text: Walk the domains, one at a time

effects.log: You walk them. The believers know you now, and bow, and offer you tea.

choices.text: Stay at the altar, and answer every petition

effects.log: There are a great many. You answer them all, slowly, and the lamp burns down.

events.text: You unfurl the banner from the roof of your hall at harvest: plain cloth, one word in black, all the kingdoms under one hand. The steward who helps you hang it asks if he may go home early, because he wants to tell his sister before the rumour reaches her. You say yes. By supper the whole valley has it.

choices.text: Let the rumour run

effects.log: It runs three kingdoms in two days. By the end of the week a king has written, in a firm hand and a trembling one.

choices.text: Write to each of the kings yourself

effects.log: You write four letters, and they are all different. The kings compare notes. They do not enjoy it.

events.text: Of sixteen regions, {auh4_held} are yours, which is to say none, and the hall has gone very quiet about it. The old minister who keeps your accounts brings a pen and one question: is this a conquest, or a rescue? You find you have not decided, and that an undecided banner is the most dangerous thing a person can fly.

choices.text: "A rescue, if they will let it be."

effects.log: The minister writes it down. Whether he believes it hardly matters, because the clerks will quote it.

choices.text: "Whichever the kingdom prefers."

effects.log: He looks as if he would like to argue, and does not, and writes it down.

events.text: The column leaves your gate in good order at first light: drums, mule-carts, sixty pupils in new boots. The road to {auh4_region} runs between fields where the farmers stop work to watch. A small boy asks his mother if you are the king. She says no, and pulls him close, and doesn't look away.

choices.text: Wave to the boy

effects.log: He waves back with both arms. His mother bows. It is a very small moment, and you will keep it.

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the road

effects.log: The road is long. At the next ford you find that someone has laid a plank over the worst of it. You never learn who.

events.text: The first night out, the school cook produces a stew that has simmered six hours and is better than anything served at a king's table. The column eats in silence. Someone starts to sing, quietly, a song of the old harvest. By the third verse the whole camp is at it, and the guards on watch hum along.

choices.text: Sing with them

effects.log: You are not good at it. They do not seem to mind. It is the last unhurried evening of the campaign.

choices.text: Listen from the tent door

effects.log: You listen, and make notes of the stragglers. It is a different sort of pleasure.

events.text: A letter from {auh4_foe}, who holds {auh4_region}, is waiting at the border post. It is brief and very polite: the ford is unguarded, the bridges sound, the wells clean. The sender does not want anyone starving or drowning on the way. You read it twice looking for the trick, and find that the trick is that there is no trick.

choices.text: Take the offered ford, and say thank you

effects.log: You do. At the far bank the scouts of {auh4_foe} salute from a distance, formally, and withdraw.

choices.text: March by the hill road regardless

effects.log: It is slower, harder, and safe from any courtesy. The column grumbles, and arrives rested enough.

events.text: The campaign wears into a second year. {auh4_foe} holds the river forts, your column holds the plain, and between you lies a lot of mud and a mutual dislike of the weather. The pupils make a game of the sentries. Your steward says there is a low point in the wall at the north bend, and that you might press, hold, or simply be kind to the village under it.

choices.text: Press the north bend before the river rises

effects.log: You press. It is taken, with a lot of mud and fewer losses than feared, and the river forts are shaken.

choices.text: Hold the line, and let them tire

effects.log: It is an untidy winter. In spring their granaries are the thinner. Nothing is celebrated.

choices.text: Spare the village under the wall

effects.log: You send a herald with a white cloth and a sack of seed. The village sends back bread and a map of the wall.

events.text: A beaten company of {auh4_power} is brought into camp at dusk: forty men and women in torn livery who walked out of their last battle through a gap in the line. They say they are tired of it. The oldest, a sergeant with a grey moustache, says they will fight again if ordered, and asks that it not be tomorrow.

choices.text: Feed them, and march at dawn

effects.log: They eat, and sleep, and in the morning they march with you, not quite willingly and not quite not.

choices.text: Let them go home, with their weapons

effects.log: They go home. A farm that had stopped producing grain begins again before the next rain.

choices.text: Keep them as a reserve, and see what happens

effects.log: They hold the rear. When the river rises they are the ones who cut the dike. You owe them for that.

events.text: Rain in the second summer, for forty days. The roads are rivers, the camp a lake. A pupil of eleven falls ill with swamp fever, and the camp physician says she can be saved by moving to high ground, which lies in the enemy line. The pupils turn to look at you. The column does not move until you say.

choices.text: March to the high ground, and fight for it

effects.log: It is the hardest fight of the year, and the girl lives. The pupils are devoted to you for life.

choices.text: Stay, and carry the girl up by hand

effects.log: It takes forty people and a long night. She lives. The column stays where it is.

choices.text: Send a truce flag for the high ground

effects.log: The answer is a polite yes. The girl is saved, and the line is not broken.

events.text: The gates of {auh4_region} open before dawn. {auh4_foe} hands over the keys in the courtyard, ring after ring, before a hundred townsfolk turned out in their best. A child has been taught a speech and gives it very fast, bowing at each pause. You thank her seriously. She is delighted.

choices.text: Return the biggest key, for safe keeping

effects.log: The old steward takes it as if it were a baby. The town is yours, and you know it is also theirs.

choices.text: Ask for the child's speech again, slowly

effects.log: She gives it again, slowly, with feeling. You carry it with you for the rest of the campaign.

events.text: {auh4_region} is yours, and {auh4_held} of sixteen now stand under the banner. The town celebrates, or does its best: a market is called, a band is found, and thrifty vendors lower their prices in your honour. The old miller says you can have his best flour free if you will promise to build a new mill-race.

choices.text: Promise it, and write it down

effects.log: You write it. In six months the mill-race is built. The miller sends you flour for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Pay for the flour, and decline the promise

effects.log: You pay. The miller is oddly hurt, and says so, and you apologise.

events.text: Half the garrison of {auh4_region} asks to join you on the day it falls. Your veterans are dubious. A boy of seventeen explains, with some heat, that he was only ever guarding his mother's house, and a veteran of {auh4_power} lowers his eyes and does not argue. The column is not sure what to do with them.

choices.text: Put them in the front rank, as proof

effects.log: They stand in the front rank, grimly and steadily. By the end of the year their names are on the roll like everyone else's.

choices.text: Send them home with a day's pay

effects.log: They go home, and what they tell their neighbours is that you let them. The next town opens its gate early.

events.text: The campaign ends badly: a flooded ford, a broken line, a dozen carts lost to the mud. {auh4_foe} sends a letter with an exact count, polite to the last digit. You are alive. The banner is rolled and leaning in the corner of the tent. You sit with it a long time, and the camp is very quiet.

choices.text: Answer the count, name by name

effects.log: You do. It does not change the figures. It changes the one who writes them.

choices.text: Hang the banner back up, a little lower

effects.log: It is a small gesture, and the pupils notice. Some take more heart from the lower banner than they ever did from the high.

events.text: Your column is scattered across three valleys, and the only road home runs through {auh4_region}. The pupils straggle back in twos and threes, wet and ashamed. The last to arrive is an old cook who was never meant to come at all, with a wounded boy on her back, apologising for the delay.

choices.text: Tell her the delay was no fault of hers

effects.log: She weeps, which you did not expect. The boy lives. Nobody else in the camp can quite look at them.

choices.text: Order a feast anyway

effects.log: There is nothing to feast on. There is a feast. People remember that you tried.

events.text: {auh4_power} counters you with such precision that you spend a week going back over your own plan. On the seventh night, in the margin of your last dispatch, you find a note in a hand you do not know: a date, a name, and the word "later". You turn the paper over. The back is blank.

choices.text: Keep the note, and watch the date

effects.log: The date passes. Nothing happens. It remains a very peculiar thing to have.

choices.text: Burn the dispatch, and plan again

effects.log: You start fresh, quickly and cleanly. It is almost pleasant.

events.text: The royal city of {auh4_power} has its gates open, its streets swept, and a single chair set on the market square under the clock. {auh4_foe} sits in it with a pot of tea and a plain sword across the knees. No soldiers. The citizens watch from windows. One gesture is being offered: a chance to refuse the war, or end it, in the open air.

choices.text: Cross the square and take the chair

ok.log: The square rings with the exchange. When it ends the clock strikes, and the windows fill with applause and weeping together.

fail.log: You cross the square, and the square does not let you across. The chair stays where it is. The clock strikes a long, mocking hour.

choices.text: Sit across the table, and speak of terms

effects.log: The tea is stone cold. The terms are written on the back of a market receipt, and they are good terms.

events.text: {auh4_foe} lets you in without a fight: the high gate, the long street, the palace stair, all of it open, all of it lit. At the top stands the throne with a plain sword leaning on it. A chamberlain whispers that the sword was left for you to choose, and that before you touch it you must decide whether you mean to take what it guards.

choices.text: Take the sword and the throne together

ok.log: The blade is lighter than it looks. {auh4_foe} bows in the old style, and the hall exhales.

fail.log: You take the sword, and the sword takes you. It is not a battle so much as a lesson in how little you know.

choices.text: Leave the sword, and ask for terms

effects.log: The chamberlain hides a smile. The terms are fair, and the sword goes back to its place.

events.text: The outer kingdoms have fallen in the field, and the royal city of {auh4_power} stands almost empty. You enter at dusk with your steward and a lantern. The throne room is cold. {auh4_foe} left in the night, and the palace cat sits on the throne, regarding you with deep suspicion. You apologise to the cat.

choices.text: Hang the banner over the throne, beside the cat

effects.log: The cat tolerates it. The steward is overcome. The rest of the evening is decidedly unceremonious.

choices.text: Read the names of the fallen from the steps

effects.log: It takes an hour. The old gate-keeper stays to the end and takes off his hat.

events.text: The capital opens to you without a blow. The palace guard stacked their weapons by the gate and went home to eat. On the throne lies a letter in a firm hand: {auh4_foe} takes the blame for everything and asks only that the household be spared. You read it twice. It is a heavy thing to find in a warm room.

choices.text: Spare the household, and keep the letter

effects.log: You post a notice at every gate. The letter goes into your coat and does not leave.

choices.text: Seek out the writer, quietly

effects.log: You find them two valleys over, mending a gate. You say nothing. You leave a loaf on the post.

events.text: A region you hold, {auh4_region}, has risen. The banner has been cut from the market mast, a green one hung in its place, and your small garrison is sitting on the town well with its boots off. The headman has put out a plain statement. They would like to be asked, next time. It is quite a good statement.

choices.text: Send the column, and take the mast down

effects.log: The column goes. The green cloth is cut, and nothing else. The next year is quiet, with a bruise in it.

choices.text: Go yourself, and sit with the headman

effects.log: You sit in his kitchen for two days. The town keeps its own flag, you keep the road, and no one calls it a victory.

choices.text: Ask the garrison what they did first

effects.log: They were stealing apples. You say so publicly, and replace the whole garrison.

events.text: The markets of {auh4_region} have gone silent. Nobody is buying from your assessors and nobody is selling. The assessors, mostly honest clerks, are fed enormous polite dinners by people who then do not speak to them. By the third week the clerks are fat and miserable and the taxes unpaid. It is the most civilised revolt in history.

choices.text: Send soldiers to collect the taxes

effects.log: The taxes arrive. So does a notice, delivered by a child, that the town will remember.

choices.text: Cut the levy by a third, and say so

effects.log: You lose coin and gain goodwill. It is the better of the two.

choices.text: Send one clerk, alone and unarmed

effects.log: She comes home with half the taxes and a jar of pickles. It is a start.

events.text: A band of young students from {auh4_region} has taken over the old watchtower under blank banners. They call themselves nothing. They ask only to go home without being called deserters. Their leader, a girl of nineteen, has put the key to the tower in a teapot, and sits on the stair with the pot in her lap.

choices.text: Break the tower, and take the pot

effects.log: The tower is broken in an afternoon. The key goes into your pocket. Nobody there is ever quite the same.

choices.text: Let them leave, with their books

effects.log: They go with their books and a note. Two of them send you gifts at the next new year.

choices.text: Ask them first what the war cost

effects.log: The answer takes six hours. You can do nothing about any of it. You remember all of it.

events.text: In the empty hour between night and dawn a bell rings in the sky over your hall, one deep tone, and a stranger without a shadow stands in the courtyard. It speaks in the voice of your own making: the kingdoms are one, and your heaven has noticed. The gods you appointed, the Keeper of your Rolls and the Maker's Shadow ask whether you will kneel, or be measured.

choices.text: Kneel to your own heaven

effects.log: You kneel on the cold stone. The shadowless stranger nods. The kingdoms are at peace for a thousand years, and your name goes unspoken.

choices.text: "Tell them I am not finished."

effects.log: The stranger looks at you a very long moment. Then the bell sounds once more, and the courtyard is empty.

events.text: A hush falls over the world you made. The harvest stops. The rivers hold still. At the end of the long corridor of your hall stands a figure that looks very much like someone you used to know, and says it has come on behalf of your own heaven. Sixteen regions under one hand is not a thing a world you shaped can allow. It will wait for your answer.

choices.text: Bow, and ask what the peace will cost

effects.log: It names the price in a voice like a closing door. You pay it. The world is saved, and your name goes unspoken.

choices.text: Stand, and raise the banner higher

effects.log: The figure bows, which is worse than any threat. It rises into the dawn. Your hands shake for the rest of the evening.

events.text: On the night before, you walk your hall from the kitchen to the practice yard, and every window is lit. Your people know what is coming. An old cook leaves a bowl at your elbow without a word. The wind is strange, the stars are in a new order, and for the first time in your life you are glad of all of it.

choices.text: Spend the night with the people who stayed

effects.log: You listen until dawn. They tell you little that is wise and everything that is true. At first light you go out, lighter.

choices.text: Spend the night in the practice yard, alone

effects.log: You work through every form you know. By dawn your hands are quiet.

events.text: The baker in the village below your hall sends up a loaf at midnight with a single line chalked on the crust: "Eat first." You laugh aloud, alone on the wall. The bread is still warm. Afterwards you look down the dark spill of the valley, its few lit windows, and decide the whole long trouble was worth it for those.

choices.text: Send down a note of thanks, and keep the crust

effects.log: You write four lines. They go down in the morning bread-cart. The crust lives on a shelf for years.

choices.text: Eat the whole loaf, and sleep

effects.log: It is a practical choice. You sleep like a stone, and wake light.

events.text: {auh4_god} comes down into the courtyard in the grey before dawn, and every lamp in the hall leans away from it. It does not speak. It lifts a hand, and the floor beneath you becomes a mirror in which you see yourself young, at the first hour of the world you built. This is what it is to face your own work: the whole sky agreeing with its maker.

choices.text: Meet it on the mirror, and strike first

ok.log: The mirror cracks like ice. The god steps back one pace, the first it has ever taken backward, and the dawn shudders.

fail.log: The mirror holds. You are thrown the length of the courtyard and land on the stair, with no sword and a ringing in your teeth.

choices.text: Let it come, and break the floor under it

ok.log: You wait. It lifts its hand, and you open the world beneath its feet. It is the best thing you ever thought of.

fail.log: You wait too long. The mirror becomes a wall, and the wall a ceiling, and nobody has ever described what came next.

events.text: The second descent is quieter. {auh4_god} waits on the wall of your hall with the first light behind, and every one of your people kneels without being told. You alone are on your feet. It asks, mildly, why. You say you do not know. It is the truest thing you have said in a lifetime.

choices.text: "Because I am tired of kneeling."

ok.log: It laughs, a sound like many bells. The fight is long and entirely in the sky, and you come down in ribbons, with your heaven bowing from a cloud.

fail.log: It does not laugh. The fight is short, and ends with you on the floor of your own practice yard while your people carefully look elsewhere.

choices.text: Say nothing, and draw

ok.log: The draw is the only answer you have, and it is a good one. The cloud splits along its length, and the sky has a seam.

fail.log: You draw, and it is already inside the draw, patient as weather. Everything after is a long fall.

events.text: The third comes at night, wrapped in no light at all. Every window in the valley dims as it passes. It tells you without sound that all before it were only tests of your reach, and that it has come to measure what is left. Your people are asleep. You step out onto the wall alone.

choices.text: Meet it in the dark, and strike by ear

ok.log: There is no sight to rely on, only the old forms in the old order, and your breath. Something in the dark gives way, and a dawn begins.

fail.log: You listen so hard you hear only yourself. The dark takes the rest.

choices.text: Light every lamp in the hall at once

ok.log: The light is brief and enormous. It flinches, and in that flinch is the whole chance of the world. You take it.

fail.log: The lamps flare, then go out together, and the dark has your name.

events.text: The sky above the world you made is a plain sky now. No Keeper, no appointed gods, no Shadow. Sixteen regions under one hand and nothing above that. You stand on the wall of your hall and, for the first time, have nobody to answer to. The baker walks up the hill with a loaf and says it is on the house.

choices.text: Take the loaf, and eat it on the wall

effects.log: It is the best bread of your life. You sit until dusk and watch the sky be nothing in particular.

choices.text: Break it, and share it with the people at the gate

effects.log: The loaf feeds eleven. You do not know who it is for. Probably all of them.

events.text: Years later they will say it happened in a single morning. In truth it took eleven years and many deaths, and you remember each. But the morning is what sticks: the banner on every mast, no stranger in the courtyard, and the long clear wind that comes when nobody above is listening. You are free to leave your hall, finally. You do not.

choices.text: Stay, and keep the kingdoms as they are

effects.log: You keep them as they are, which turns out to be harder than conquering them. For a long time it is a pleasant sort of struggle.

choices.text: Walk out of the gate, and keep walking

effects.log: The kingdoms let you go. Behind you a baker lights her oven. Ahead of you is everything else.

events.text: The blow does not feel like a blow. It feels like your whole world making up its mind about you, and then quiet. You see your hall once more, small and bright, with the banner still on its mast. Someone will take that banner down tomorrow. Someone else, much later, will put it back up.

choices.text: Let go, and look at the valley

effects.log: You look at it all the way down. It is very beautiful from far enough away.

choices.text: Reach for the banner, once more

effects.log: Your hand closes on nothing. It was worth trying.

events.text: You are not killed. You are put back in your proper place, which is a good deal smaller than where you stood. The sky closes. The banner is taken down by a patient hand. Sixteen regions go back to their own, and nobody kneels, and nobody cheers. The kingdoms are all still there. Only you are different.

choices.text: Accept it, and go quietly

effects.log: You go. The kingdoms are quiet the rest of your life. Nobody speaks of it, and everybody remembers.

choices.text: Remember it, and tell the pupils

effects.log: You do. It becomes a tale. It is told wrong, and it is told for a thousand years.

events.text: The stranger dissolves into the morning, and the courtyard breathes out. Sixteen regions, one hand, and a very long peace that nobody will remember being earned. An old steward says it is what a good peace is: unremarked. A fine rain begins, the first in months. You stand in it a while.

choices.text: Stand in the rain, and let it fall

effects.log: You stand. It is a good rain. You are not unhappy, and you are not altogether sure what you are.

choices.text: Order the lamps lit in honour of the quiet

effects.log: They are lit. For a thousand years the kingdoms will light them on this night, not knowing why.

events.text: You bowed, and the sky lifted, and nothing else changed. The bakers baked, the pupils drilled, the fields were weeded. Somewhere above, a very large decision was made and written in a book you will never see. You look at your hands. They are the same hands. A year ago you could not have said this would be enough.

choices.text: Let it be enough

effects.log: It is enough. It is a long, quiet, ordinary happiness, and you are surprised how little it asks of you.

choices.text: Write the whole history down, as it was

effects.log: You write it. It is the only record of what you nearly did, and nobody reads it for centuries.

events.text: The banner comes down off the mast in one movement, and a young pupil folds it corner to corner, the way a flag is folded for a burial. The sixteen regions are released. A few cheer. A few weep. The baker looks up from her oven, nods once, and goes back to the dough.

choices.text: Keep the folded cloth

effects.log: It lives in a chest at the foot of your bed, and you look at it on certain nights.

choices.text: Give it to the pupil who folded it

effects.log: The pupil is speechless. It hangs over their door for years, as a sign of something.

events.text: You take down the banner yourself, without ceremony, in the evening. The kingdoms do not notice at first. Then a boy on the lower road sees the bare mast and puts a hand to his mouth. By midnight the whole world knows. Your steward waits to be told if it is a defeat. You tell him it is a change of weather.

choices.text: Take a long walk along the border

effects.log: You walk for three days. You come back lighter.

choices.text: Stay at your desk and answer every letter

effects.log: The letters are mostly kind. A few are not. You answer all of them.
